standard: Subscription / SaaS net & gross revenue retention corpus
source: ChartMogul / OpenView / Stripe / KeyBanc / SaaS Capital references (web-researched 2026-07-24)

entries.title: Net Revenue Retention (NRR) / Net Dollar Retention (NDR) — definition
entries.body: NRR (also called NDR or Net Dollar Retention) = (Starting MRR + Expansion − Contraction − Churned) ÷ Starting MRR × 100. It measures how existing customers' revenue compounds after expansion, contraction, and churn. Above 100% means the base grows with zero new logos.

entries.title: NDR and NRR are the same concept
entries.body: Net Dollar Retention (NDR) and Net Revenue Retention (NRR) are interchangeable labels for the same metric. Do not mistake logo/customer retention (count-based) for NRR (revenue-based) — retaining 90% of customers can coexist with weak NRR if top accounts leave.

entries.title: NRR benchmarks — what 'good' looks like
entries.body: NRR above 120% is excellent (best-in-class enterprise SaaS); 100–120% is strong; 90–100% is adequate but means new-customer growth is required to grow overall; below 90% signals a retention problem. Best-in-class often 120–150%.

entries.title: NRR percentiles by ARR band (ChartMogul SaaS Retention Report)
entries.body: Median NRR by ARR band: <$300K → 57.6%; $300K–$1M → 70.2%; $1–3M → 77.9%; $3–8M → 82.1%; $8–15M → 81.3%; $15–30M → 93.4%. B2B SaaS should target >100%; crossing 100% typically happens around $15M+ ARR.

entries.title: Gross Revenue Retention (GRR) — capped at 100%
entries.body: GRR = (Starting MRR − Contraction − Churned) ÷ Starting MRR × 100. It excludes expansion, so it is capped at 100% and isolates pure leakage. If GRR is low, expansion may be masking a real churn problem.

entries.title: GRR benchmark — ~90% median, 92%+ strong
entries.body: Median GRR ~90% (KeyBanc 2024); 92%+ is strong and 95%+ top-tier. GRR below 90% with healthy NRR means expansion is doing heavy lifting to compensate for leakage — fragile durability.

entries.title: 2026 NDR / GRR benchmarks (OpenView, Bessemer, KeyBanc, SaaS Capital)
entries.body: Aggregated 2024–2026 surveys: median NDR ~101% (KeyBanc 2024), 100% across B2B SaaS; best-in-class exceeds 110%, top-decile 120%+. GRR median ~90%. Usage-based pricing averages ~133% NRR vs ~110% seat-based. Reference ranges, not guarantees.

entries.title: NDR < 100% = 'leaky bucket'
entries.body: OpenView: an NDR below 100% means you are acquiring customers (costly) merely to disguise churn and hold top-line growth — inefficient, backfires eventually. NDR should be on everyone's mind as the foundation for weathering top-of-funnel downturns.

entries.title: NDR median 100–111% by company size (OpenView 2022 via Stripe)
entries.body: Per OpenView's 2022 report as summarized by Stripe: median NDR across SaaS companies sits between 100% and 111% depending on size. >100% indicates existing customers grow revenue (upsell/cross-sell working); ~100% stable; <100% a warning.

entries.title: Net-negative churn — the 'holy grail' of SaaS
entries.body: Net negative churn exists when expansion + reactivation MRR exceeds churned + contraction MRR, so NDR exceeds 100% without any new logos. ChartMogul calls it the only kind of churn you want — the base self-grows.

entries.title: NDR is the single most powerful SaaS health metric
entries.body: Top SaaS companies show 120–150% NRR. NDR demonstrates the product becomes more valuable over time and that growth compounds on an already-growing base — the quality signal investors weight most heavily after growth rate.

entries.title: Strict NDR formula and edge cases
entries.body: NDR = (Starting MRR + Expansion MRR − Contraction MRR − Churned MRR) ÷ Starting MRR. Use the same cohort of customers at start and end of period; exclude new-logo MRR entirely from both numerator and denominator to avoid inflating retention.
